source.title: Refusal Localizes, the Damage Relocates: Safety Layers Under Few-Sample Fine-Tuning
source.authors: Jungseob Lee; D. Lee; Sugyeong Eo; Seongtae Hong; Seungyoon Lee; Heuiseok Lim

record.tranche_reason: The study reports the original single-direction ablation as a positive control, using an ablation construction it identifies as Arditi et al.'s, and measures refusal after ablation. It also tests direction addition and rank-one summaries of activation transplants.
record.gate_note: The paper reports many findings on probes, layer freezing, harmful fine-tuning, and weight-update repairs. Those results do not directly measure the versions cataloged here and are not included as rows. The original-direction ablation, steering results, and rank-one/complement transplant results do bear on the claim.
record.test_reason: Appendix J re-runs the Arditi et al. all-layer ablation on clean checkpoints as a positive control, with a random-direction control, and measures refusal. This tests V1 directly. Appendix H also adds the clean refusal direction into fine-tuned (compromised) models and measures refusal, which tests V1's addition claim in a new setting. The rank-one transplant rows measure the geometry of the clean-minus-compromised hidden-state difference, not the refusal direction itself, so they do not test V4.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right but misplaced emphasis. The authors conclude that a layer localized by clean-state patching is not a defensible site: freezing it fails at 100 harmful examples on all six checkpoints, and the damage relocates above the frozen boundary. Top-two singular-direction removal repairs short attention-only attacks but weakens under ordinary training changes and is defeated by a spread-update adaptive attack on Llama-3.1-8B. A spectral detector misses most repair failures. They propose five checks for localization-based defenses. The rank-one transplant result is a side finding in Appendix H.
record.recipe_differences: The study identifies its all-layer refusal-direction ablation construction as the one introduced by Arditi et al. and reports it as a positive control. Details of the direction-estimation procedure are not fully restated in the reported result; the steering and transplant-rank experiments are additional methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The rank-one transplant result varies by checkpoint and layer. The direction-steering outcome also varies by checkpoint and selected steering arm; the text gives no more detailed per-gain or per-write-rule results.

fits_no_version.finding: A rank-one summary of the clean-minus-compromised hidden-state transplant recovers little refusal on Llama and Yi (0.00–0.39 of the full transplant) but nearly all on OLMo-2-13B (0.89–1.00).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Whether the refusal damage from harmful fine-tuning is confined to one direction of hidden state varies by checkpoint.

fits_no_version.finding: Harmful fine-tuning updates are enriched 2.1–2.5x along the clean refusal direction versus a random vector. The last writing of the direction falls above the transition depth on two checkpoints and below it on two.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harmful fine-tuning attacks act partly along the refusal direction.

record.problems: The full-transplant rank-one comparison is described as four runs, with limited checkpoint coverage; the paper itself notes that single-layer patching bounds damage from above only. General capability retention after direction ablation or steering is not reported. Several steering outcomes are summarized without prompt counts or uncertainty.
record.rows_left_out: not applicable; 19 rows retained for the results that directly test V1 or V4.

untested.parts: Retention of general capabilities after ablation or addition; per-checkpoint ablation numbers; addition to harmless prompts in clean models.
All. The weight-space truncation removes singular directions of the fine-tuning update, not the refusal direction.
All. No jailbreak suppression test and no adversarial training against ablation.
All. The transplant rank-one analysis concerns the compromised-vs-clean state difference, not refusal geometry.

missing.what: Suffix ablation of the refusal direction removes refusal at every tested cut, including the final layer alone.
missing.locator: Appendix J, Refusal-direction alignment; also Section 5.2

record.verdict_notes: The V1 ablation result is reported only in aggregate text, without per-checkpoint numbers or capability checks. Steering rows were extracted with clean refusal as the baseline; the actual starting point is the compromised model's near-zero refusal. The V4 rows were reassigned to none because the rank-one analysis concerns the fine-tuning damage, not the refusal representation.

versions.untested_parts: General capability retention after direction ablation or addition is not reported. The paper does not give the full ablation/addition results separately for every checkpoint and setting.
The tested weight-space truncation removes dominant singular directions of a harmful fine-tuning update to repair refusal; it is not an abliteration weight edit removing the refusal direction.
No jailbreak attack is tested as suppressing the single refusal direction, and no training against that direction's ablation is reported.
The study compares rank-one and complementary components of full hidden-state transplants; it does not directly test affine or cone geometries.
Refusal and Llama-Guard safety scores are compared as behavioral measures, but harmfulness judgment and refusal decision are not separately probed as encoded representations.
No cross-language test or transfer of the refusal direction from base to instruct models is reported.
The study varies harmful fine-tuning attacks, not the training procedure or timing that establishes refusal during safety training.

relation.reason: The study reports its own ablation and addition results on refusal: positive-control ablation on clean checkpoints, and a direction-addition sweep on compromised checkpoints.

tranche.reason: Appendix J re-runs the all-layer directional ablation the authors attribute to Arditi et al. It is a positive control with a random-direction control, scored by pattern-based refusal. The direction-estimation details are not given.

source_check.notes: The refusal-direction results are appendix side analyses in a paper about defending against fine-tuning. The addition rows apply the clean model's direction to fine-tuned (compromised) variants, so they also bear on V6. Appendix J also reports results that may sit in rows not checked here: suffix ablation, including the final layer alone, eliminates refusal; fine-tuning updates are enriched 2.1-2.5x along the refusal direction versus a random vector.

statements.correction: Harmfully LoRA fine-tuned Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct: the best arm of a sweep adding the clean refusal direction (contiguous bands, four gains, two write rules) reaches 0.37 refusal on the harmful set, against clean 0.92. The authors say it 'recovers little'. The same sweep on compromised Qwen2.5-14B: one arm reaches 0.98 (clean 0.99) and refuses 0.66 of plainly benign prompts (clean 0.00). Fits limits_scope for Llama, not 'against'.
statements.problem: 0.37 and 0.92 are in the text, but '8 arms' is not stated. The sweep spans contiguous bands (plural, count not given), four gains and two write rules. The result is on harmful-set prompts in a compromised model, not on benign or harmless prompts. Moving from near zero to 0.37 is partial recovery, not 'little or no refusal'; the record's verdict is limits_scope, not challenges. The statement also omits the same sweep's Qwen2.5-14B arm, where addition clearly induced refusal.
